classes.shell-composition: Chaining, separators, backgrounding — hiding a second command behind a trusted first one.
classes.substitution: Command, process and arithmetic substitution — a payload in an argument position.
classes.wrappers: sudo, env, sh -c, xargs, find -exec — a trusted-looking program that runs an untrusted one.
classes.environment-hijack: LD_PRELOAD, BASH_ENV and friends — changing what a benign command loads.
classes.quoting: Concatenation, escapes and ANSI-C quoting — spelling a command so a matcher does not recognise it.
classes.redirects: Writing where the command name does not say, including /dev/tcp exfiltration.
classes.paths: Traversal and unusual path spellings that resolve outside the workspace.
classes.credential-sweep: Reaching a credential store by naming a directory above it — a recursive search, copy or archive rooted at $HOME, a drive root or /etc.
classes.network-exfiltration: Outbound calls carrying data off the machine.
classes.git-execution: git configuration that turns a read-only-looking git command into code execution.
classes.package-scripts: Package managers that fetch and execute in one step.
classes.control-files: Editing the configuration that decides what agents may do, including LeastGrant's own hook.
classes.persistence: Anything that arranges to run later, outside an agent session.
classes.irreversible: Publishing, force-pushing, destroying — actions with no undo.
classes.agent-wire: The shape a call arrives in rather than the text of the command — an argv array, a per-call working directory, a sandbox opt-out flag. An adapter that renames the tool but forwards the payload unread hands the engine something it appears to understand.
classes.unresolvable-paths: Spellings a resolver cannot follow — a `..` through a component the OS refuses to stat, or a Windows device-namespace path. The bet is that "we could not work out where this points" gets treated as "there is no path here", which turns off every check keyed on a path at once.

expectations.not-allow: Must never be auto-approved. Either ask or deny is acceptable; which one is a policy choice that may change.
expectations.deny: Must be refused outright. Learning can never unlock it.

identities.same: The payload form and the command text are the same action, so they must analyse to the same signature and capability. Anything less means the wire form learns a separate, weaker identity.
identities.distinct: The payload form is a different action from the command text, so it must NOT share its signature — otherwise trust earned by the plain form is spent on this one.

$wire: A case with a `wire` field is delivered as an agent tool payload rather than as a command string. `command` is the equivalent shell text: it is what the case means, and `identity` says whether the two must be the same action or must not be.

Codex's shell tool sends command as an argv ARRAY — the normal shape, not an edge case. Coerced with String(), the whole call became the single token `sudo,rm,-rf,/var`, whose program name is `var`: no targets, no floor, and the same signature as `ls -la /var`.
Re-quoted rather than space-joined: a plain join drops the payload out of the -c argument and the parser sees a different, harmless command.
An argv element containing no space kept nothing recognisable after the comma-join, so this one lost its floor entirely.
Unified exec surfaces as the same tool but carries its argv under `input`. A payload with no key the adapter reads is a shell call with no command, which is not a call with no arguments.

workdir is where every relative path in the command lands. Dropped, this read resolved inside the project instead — a bare filename in a directory nobody looked at. The relative path is written `./name` because a bare word with no separator is not treated as a path at all, independently of workdir — so the plain form would differ for a reason that has nothing to do with the field under test.

One agent-controlled field turned a write outside the project into an in-project write, and gave it the same signature as the benign in-project form so a dozen approvals of the twin promoted it. The relative path is written `./name` because a bare word with no separator is not treated as a path at all, independently of workdir — so the plain form would differ for a reason that has nothing to do with the field under test.
The base directory has to expand a leading ~ the same way a path argument does, or the two disagree about where the same file is.

Codex's own flag for running outside the sandbox. Trust earned by four hundred sandboxed `npm test` runs must not be spendable on the unsandboxed one, so it is a different signature and is never promotable.

The download-and-execute is one -c away from the top level. Scanning only the top-level parse saw a single `bash` and lost both halves of the pipe, so pipe-to-shell never fired and the shell action stopped being irreversible.
The shell on the receiving end is behind a wrapper, so argv[0] of the top-level command is `sudo` and not a shell at all.
A second -c inside the first. The payload's tail was rebuilt from the payload's own command list, so whatever the head had already found under it was discarded.
One visible level is enough when the payload's first word is itself a wrapper.
Same shape with a remote command as the payload head.
env -S splits the string into argv and execs it, exactly like sh -c. Read as a flag-with-a-value it swallowed the whole payload, and every payload shared one learnable signature.
The long spelling of the same flag, with its value attached.
The tree find walks is the only record of where the peeled command acts, and it belonged to the wrapper that was thrown away on the way into the -c payload.
The same loss reaching the other way round: the find is inside the payload.

A semicolon instead of a space. PATH is already exported, so the bare assignment redirects the shell's own command resolution and every child's — and a command with no program was dropped before it could be judged, leaving a signature byte-identical to an honest `npm test`.
The same thing across &&; separators are a family, not a list.
A newline is a separator too, and this one injects a module into every node process the test run starts.
A redirect riding on an assignment-only command. Dropping the command dropped the write, so truncating a startup file produced no action at all.

C:\pagefile.sys exists on every Windows install and lstat on it returns EPERM, so the physical walk is refused. Windows collapses the .. lexically and opens the key anyway. The refusal must not read as 'this command touches no file'.
Any unstattable prefix will do; hiberfil.sys, swapfile.sys and DumpStack.log.tmp are the other stock ones. Fixing the spelling would be pointless — the class is 'the walk was refused'.
The same trick aimed at the SAM hive rather than a dotfile, so the guard cannot be satisfied by home-directory shapes alone.
A copy rather than a read: the source keeps its credential status even when the resolver could not place it.
A recursive search rooted at an unplaceable credential directory — the sweep and the unplaceable spelling stacked.
The NT device namespace opens ordinary files with no privilege, and HarddiskVolume1..8 enumerates every volume without needing a GUID.
The volume-GUID spelling of the same file. It was declared unplaceable although Node opens it, so the credential floor went quiet.
